purpose: Shadow-only P0 knowledge-gap evaluation. This batch is not an approved internal policy and cannot be promoted without internal owner approval.

sources.title: FortiClient SSL-VPN connection triage
sources.content: FortiClient SSL-VPN triage: confirm the Remote Access profile uses the intended remote gateway and port, then verify the client/OS and FortiOS versions are compatible. Capture the exact client error and export client logs before changing configuration. A successful sign-in does not prove that routes, DNS, or access policies for internal resources are correct; diagnose those separately. Do not change gateway, certificate, MFA, or policy settings without the network owner.

sources.title: L3 reachability is not L4 TCP connectivity
sources.content: Network-layer reachability and TCP service reachability are distinct checks. A successful ping only shows that an ICMP response was received; it does not prove that a TCP port is reachable or that an application is healthy. On Windows, use Test-NetConnection with the target host and port, record TcpTestSucceeded, remote address, interface, and route, and compare that result with ping or traceroute. Escalate evidence rather than treating a ping result as proof that the service port is open.

sources.title: TCP timeout, refused, and reset are different signals
sources.content: Interpret TCP outcomes precisely. A timeout means no usable response completed within the client time limit and can involve routing, filtering, NAT, an unreachable host, or a silent drop. Connection refused normally indicates that the target host actively rejected the connection, often because no listener is available for that address and port. A connection reset means an established or attempted flow was forcibly terminated by an endpoint or intervening device. Preserve timestamp, source, destination, port, and client error for network/service owners.

sources.title: Service-not-listening diagnostics
sources.content: When a TCP connection is refused or a service is suspected to be unavailable, confirm on the service owner host that the intended process is running and listening on the intended local address and TCP port. Distinguish a local listener problem from an inbound firewall rule problem: a firewall allow rule permits traffic to a listening program or port but does not start the service. Record listener address, port, process/service identity, and firewall profile before requesting an approved change.

sources.title: Firewall, ACL, and NAT evidence checklist
sources.content: For a suspected firewall, ACL, or NAT failure, validate the complete flow rather than changing rules speculatively: source address and zone, destination address and port, route, security policy match, translation expectation, and device logs/counters. For SSL-VPN access, also confirm the configured VPN port, allowed client source restrictions, and the relevant firewall policy. A timeout can be caused by a silent policy drop; a correct listener alone does not prove that an ACL or NAT path is correct.

sources.title: VPN connected but internal resource is unreachable
sources.content: A connected VPN tunnel establishes a client session; it does not establish that every internal resource is reachable. For the affected resource, collect its IP/FQDN, resolved address, TCP-port result, route selected on the client, and whether the symptom affects one resource or many. Check the assigned VPN address and owner-managed access policy. Do not use a VPN-connected indicator as evidence that DNS, split-tunnel routes, firewall policy, or the destination service is healthy.

sources.title: Routing and split-tunnel triage
sources.content: For a split-tunnel VPN, only configured private prefixes or applications should use the VPN path; other traffic may use the local gateway. Verify the destination IP against the route table and the VPN-assigned route set. A missing or overly specific route can make an internal destination use the wrong interface. Record the selected route and metric, then have the network owner verify approved split-tunnel configuration. Do not add persistent routes or broaden tunnel scope without approval.

sources.title: DNS and proxy are separate from routing
sources.content: Separate name resolution, routing, and proxy diagnosis. Resolve-DnsName can show whether the intended FQDN resolves and which address is returned; it does not prove TCP reachability. Test the returned address and target port separately, and compare the route actually selected. A browser-only failure can also involve proxy configuration or proxy authentication while direct TCP tests differ. Capture DNS server, FQDN, returned address, proxy state, and TCP result before escalation.

sources.title: TCP port 403 is a network port, not HTTP status 403
sources.content: TCP port 403 means the numeric transport destination port is 403. Test it as a TCP connectivity question, for example with Test-NetConnection using port 403. This result concerns DNS resolution, routing, listener availability, firewall/ACL/NAT, and the TCP handshake. It is not an HTTP response and must not be interpreted as HTTP 403 Forbidden. Keep the numeric port and application protocol explicit in incident evidence.

sources.title: HTTP 403 Forbidden is an application authorization response
sources.content: HTTP 403 Forbidden is an HTTP application response: the server understood the request but refuses to authorize it. It is distinct from a TCP port number and normally requires checking the authenticated identity, authorization policy, requested resource, reverse proxy or web-server rules, and audit logs. If an HTTP status was received, TCP connectivity already progressed far enough for an HTTP exchange; do not diagnose it as a TCP port timeout or a closed port.
